records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field lists three entries — 'Christmas Dagger', 'Christmas Dagger Fern', 'Christmas Fern' — alphabetized and in the same order as the page title's parenthetical; 'Christmas Fern' is the third of the three. NC State's own body-prose Description nonetheless opens 'Christmas fern is a rhizomatous, densely scaly-scruffy, evergreen herbaceous perennial in the polypody family (Polypodiaceae).' RHS's page title reads 'Polystichum acrostichoides | Christmas fern', its Plant Profile subtitle gives 'Christmas fern', and its 'Other common names' field reads 'Christmas fern, dagger fern'. MoBot's Common Name field gives 'Christmas fern'. RHS and MoBot both lead with Christmas fern and NC State's prose uses it, so Christmas Fern is taken as the lead common name; 'Christmas Dagger' is NC State's alphabetically-first structured entry and 'dagger fern' is RHS's second listed alternate.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's plant-record tags scope non-toxicity to cats, dogs, and horses specifically: the record carries the tags "#non-toxic for cats#non-toxic for horses#non-toxic for dogs". The page's Whole Plant Traits/Plant Type field lists only Fern, Native Plant, Perennial — it does not carry a "Poisonous" plant-type value or a "Poisonous to Humans" problem tag, so there is no structured Poison block (severity, symptoms, toxic principle, or poison-part list) to report for this species. No other admissible source addresses toxicity for this species.

NC State's page H1 is the binomial Adiantum pedatum, and its Common Name(s) field lists three alphabetized entries -- Common Maidenhair; Northern Maidenhair; Northern Maidenhair Fern -- so its first entry is 'Common Maidenhair' and the name used here is its third. Northern Maidenhair Fern is used as common_name on the strength of MoBot's lead value, backed by NC State's list entry and body prose; it is distinct from the houseplant Adiantum raddianum already in this catalog under 'Maidenhair Fern'.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists four alphabetized entries -- Fiddlehead Fern, Ostrich-Feather Fern, Ostrich Fern, Shuttlecock Fern -- in the same order as its page-title parenthetical; its first entry is Fiddlehead Fern and its rendered H1 is the binomial alone, though its Description prose opens 'Ostrich fern is an easy-to-grow, herbaceous perennial fern...'. Missouri Botanical Garden renders a single field, 'Common Name: ostrich fern'; a 'Common Names' hover control beside it holds a three-name list, but that text lives only in the link's overlib attribute and is therefore not quoted. Penn State Extension's article is titled 'Native Plants of PA: Ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris)'. RHS carries 'shuttlecock fern' as the subtitle under its binomial heading and lists 'ostrich fern, ostrich-feather fern' under Other common names. common_name follows MoBot's Common Name field and Penn State's title, the two sources that lead with it; RHS's competing lead is Shuttlecock Fern and NC State's list leads with Fiddlehead Fern. Separately, NC State treats Onoclea struthiopteris as accepted, listing Matteuccia nodulosa, Matteuccia struthiopteris and Struthiopteris cordi under 'Previously known as:', while RHS's Name Status field reads 'Correct' for Matteuccia struthiopteris; scientific_name_accepted follows RHS.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source states any toxicity scoped to cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets is left null; NC State's page carries no Poison Part or Poison Severity field, and neither MoBot nor RHS carries any toxicity section. The only toxicity statement found is Penn State Extension's human food-safety caution about the edible fiddleheads: 'CAUTION: Tender fiddleheads of ostrich fern are TOXIC if not fully cooked. When properly prepared, fiddleheads have a taste similar to that of asparagus.' The same page frames the fiddleheads as a wild food -- 'Fiddleheads of ostrich fern, along with other members of the genera Matteuccia, Osmundastrum, and Pteridium, can be harvested as a wild food. This document does not provide guidance on edible wild plants or foraging.' -- and gives no cooking method or time. Sources disagree on framing: NC State's structured Edibility field reads only 'Fiddleheads can be cooked and consumed' and its tag list includes '#edible', with no raw-toxicity caution.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS, Penn State) frames any toxicity statement as scoped to cats or dogs specifically; NC State's page for this species carries no Poison Part/Poison Severity fields at all. Only a human food-safety caution about undercooked fiddleheads was found (Penn State), which per the cat/dog scoping rule cannot support toxic_to_pets=true.
